messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Reyes, a 34-year-old Navy officer, had always taken pride in being steady under pressure, the sort of man who could keep others calm. That changed after the hurricane evacuation mission he led from a flooded coastal town, when the power failed, the streets filled with debris and shouting, and people pressed shoulder to shoulder in the dark while fuel, saltwater, and spilled alcohol from a looted shop hung in the air. He later described the scene in fragments rather than a smooth account: flashes of headlights sweeping across water, arms reaching, bodies packed tight in hallways, and the stunned moment of realizing how little control he had over who got out and who did not. Since then, crowded places have felt dangerous in a way he cannot shake, and even a grocery aisle or a busy marina can make him scan for exits and feel boxed in. Physical locations with narrow passages or dim corners, especially being in the dark, have become hard to tolerate, and the smell of alcohol can stop him cold because it brings back the reek that seemed to cling to the evacuation site.

When these reminders hit, Daniel has found himself shutting down parts of his life. He avoids seeing friends because he does not want to be caught off guard in a restaurant or bar, and he has turned down invitations from shipmates more often than he admits at home. He tells himself he deserves to suffer for what happened, as if enduring discomfort is the least he can do after surviving while others were trapped in that chaos. That kind of self-punishment has narrowed his world, but it also keeps him away from crowded rooms and the kinds of circumstances that might pull him back into that night.

What tends to come back first is not a full story but images: a lantern-lit stairwell, the crush of people, the look on a child’s face. Daniel says the memory is mostly pictures or images, and when it arrives it is so extreme that it feels hard to believe it actually happened to him. At those moments, his body seems to drop back into the same position it was in during the evacuation, shoulders tight and chest braced as if he is still wedged among panicked bodies. Those bodily flashes leave him feeling that the event is not really over, and that sense of unreality deepens his conviction that he must somehow be changed by it. He has come to believe he is no longer the happy person he used to be, that misery has become his baseline, and that he no longer belongs anywhere. Around other people he feels isolated and set apart, even among fellow officers who once felt like his closest circle, because they seem to belong to a world he can no longer enter.

Those appraisals feed the memories back again. When he thinks, with a kind of bitter certainty, that he is permanently different and cut off from everyone else, the images return sharper and more invasive, as if the mind is offering proof. The same thoughts also make the reminders in daily life hit harder: a crowded elevator on base, a dark parking garage, or the sharp smell of liquor at a hotel function can all feel like confirmation that the disaster is still close enough to reach him. He then tightens his routine further, passing up social plans, avoiding places that remind him of the evacuation, and telling himself the restriction is deserved. Yet the more he withdraws, the more the old pictures crowd him when he is alone, and the more those images make ordinary settings feel threatening again. Even brief memories of the crush and darkness can make him avoid the very situations that might otherwise reassure him, while the avoidance itself leaves him with more time to replay the event and more occasions to notice the cues that set it off.

By the time Daniel sought help, his wife had noticed how much of the week he spent keeping to himself and how quickly he went tense in crowded or dim places. He came in saying he was tired of living as if he had already been judged and found guilty, and he was most afraid that the life he had built with his wife and in the Navy would keep shrinking until there was nothing left that felt like his own.
